terraform-aiven.wrapped_text:
Terraform for Aiven
The Aiven provider lets Terraform
manage Aiven projects, services
and the objects inside services.
Aiven maintains it under the
source address `aiven/aiven`
([provider docs](https://registry.
terraform.io/providers/aiven/aiven
/latest/docs)). The provider calls
the Aiven API with an API token
([provider configuration](https://
github.com/aiven/terraform-provide
r-aiven/blob/v4.66.0/internal/plug
in/provider.go#L71-L83)). It does
not connect to Kafka as a client.
The [Kafka map](../../kafka/kafka.
md#aiven-aiven) explains what
Aiven runs, and the [Terraform
map](../terraform.md) explains
Terraform itself.

The unit is one Aiven project and
the services in it. Aiven groups
everything in three levels: an
organization holds projects, and a
project holds services ([Projects
and Services](../../kafka/kafka.md
#projects-and-services-aiven-proje
cts-services)). A service is one
running product, such as a Kafka
cluster or a Kafka Connect
cluster. Inside a Kafka service
live the objects that a data
engineer touches most: topics,
access rules, schemas and
connectors.

Each object has its own resource,
and each resource has one key
idea:

- A service is a machine with
data. Its name is its identity, so
a new name means a new, empty
service ([A Service Holds Data](#a
-service-holds-data-a-service-hold
s-data)).
- The advanced settings of a
service only grow. Removing a
setting from the code leaves the
live value in place ([Service
Settings Only Grow](#service-setti
ngs-only-grow-service-settings-onl
y-grow)).
- A topic is known by its name. A
new name means a new, empty topic
([The Topic Name Is the Key](#the-
topic-name-is-the-key-the-topic-na
me-is-the-key)).
- A connector is a flat map of
strings that the provider hardly
checks ([A Connector Is a Map of S
trings](#a-connector-is-a-map-of-s
trings-a-connector-is-a-map-of-str
ings)).
- A schema subject is a list of
versions that only grows ([Schema
Subjects Only Grow](#schema-subjec
ts-only-grow-schema-subjects-only-
grow)).
- Aiven has two kinds of access
rule, and both can apply to one
user ([Two ACL Models](#two-acl-mo
dels-two-acl-models)).

Two more ideas explain surprising
plans. The provider is built on
two Terraform libraries, and each
resource behaves like its library
([Two Libraries in One Provider](#
two-libraries-in-one-provider-two-
libraries-in-one-provider)). Aiven
also changes some things on its
own, outside any plan ([Aiven
Changes Things Too](#aiven-changes
-things-too-aiven-changes-things-t
oo)).

Now compare the Snowflake
provider. Both manage a service
that someone else runs.
Snowflake's provider speaks SQL,
and Aiven's provider speaks REST.
In both, the most dangerous line
in a plan is a replacement of an
object that holds data.

The map has four parts. Mental
Models explains the ideas above.
Reading an Aiven Configuration
says what you will see and where
to look first. Pitfalls lists the
failures that experienced users
plan around. Good and Bad
Decisions compares the common
design choices.

Terraform for Aiven
The Aiven provider lets Terraform manage Aiven projects, services and the objects inside services. Aiven maintains it under the source address `aiven/aiven` ([provider docs](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/aiven/aiven/latest/docs)). The provider calls the Aiven API with an API token ([provider configuration](https://github.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/v4.66.0/internal/plugin/provider.go#L71-L83)). It does not connect to Kafka as a client. The [Kafka map](../../kafka/kafka.md#aiven-aiven) explains what Aiven runs, and the [Terraform map](../terraform.md) explains Terraform itself.

The unit is one Aiven project and the services in it. Aiven groups everything in three levels: an organization holds projects, and a project holds services ([Projects and Services](../../kafka/kafka.md#projects-and-services-aiven-projects-services)). A service is one running product, such as a Kafka cluster or a Kafka Connect cluster. Inside a Kafka service live the objects that a data engineer touches most: topics, access rules, schemas and connectors.

Each object has its own resource, and each resource has one key idea:

- A service is a machine with data. Its name is its identity, so a new name means a new, empty service ([A Service Holds Data](#a-service-holds-data-a-service-holds-data)).
- The advanced settings of a service only grow. Removing a setting from the code leaves the live value in place ([Service Settings Only Grow](#service-settings-only-grow-service-settings-only-grow)).
- A topic is known by its name. A new name means a new, empty topic ([The Topic Name Is the Key](#the-topic-name-is-the-key-the-topic-name-is-the-key)).
- A connector is a flat map of strings that the provider hardly checks ([A Connector Is a Map of Strings](#a-connector-is-a-map-of-strings-a-connector-is-a-map-of-strings)).
- A schema subject is a list of versions that only grows ([Schema Subjects Only Grow](#schema-subjects-only-grow-schema-subjects-only-grow)).
- Aiven has two kinds of access rule, and both can apply to one user ([Two ACL Models](#two-acl-models-two-acl-models)).

Two more ideas explain surprising plans. The provider is built on two Terraform libraries, and each resource behaves like its library ([Two Libraries in One Provider](#two-libraries-in-one-provider-two-libraries-in-one-provider)). Aiven also changes some things on its own, outside any plan ([Aiven Changes Things Too](#aiven-changes-things-too-aiven-changes-things-too)).

Now compare the Snowflake provider. Both manage a service that someone else runs. Snowflake's provider speaks SQL, and Aiven's provider speaks REST. In both, the most dangerous line in a plan is a replacement of an object that holds data.

The map has four parts. Mental Models explains the ideas above. Reading an Aiven Configuration says what you will see and where to look first. Pitfalls lists the failures that experienced users plan around. Good and Bad Decisions compares the common design choices.

a-service-holds-data.wrapped_text:
A Service Holds Data
An `aiven_kafka` or `aiven_kafka_connect`
resource stands for a service: machines, disks
and the software on them. A change of
`service_name` or `project` replaces the
service. The provider's own docs warn that the
service and all its data are deleted before
Aiven creates the new one ([provider warning](
https://github.com/aiven/terraform-provider-ai
ven/blob/v4.66.0/docs/index.md#L43-L47)).

The same page asks you to set
`termination_protection = true` on every
production service. Aiven itself enforces this
flag, so it also blocks a delete from the
console or the CLI. It does not protect topics
or other objects inside the service ([terminat
ion_protection](https://github.com/aiven/terra
form-provider-aiven/blob/v4.66.0/docs/resource
s/kafka.md#L69)).

The children of a service, such as topics,
ACLs and connectors, name the service in
`project` and `service_name`. Those two fields
force a replacement on each child too. So a
replaced service also replaces everything
inside it.

service-settings-only-grow.wrapped_text:
Service Settings Only Grow
A Kafka service has a block of advanced
settings, `kafka_user_config`. It holds broker
defaults, the Kafka version, and switches for
Kafka Connect, the Schema Registry and the
REST proxy. The provider warns: "There's no
way to reset advanced configuration options to
default. Options that you add cannot be
removed later" ([kafka_user_config](https://gi
thub.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/v
4.66.0/docs/resources/kafka.md#L60)).

So the code shows only the settings that
someone added and kept. A setting that someone
removed from the code still runs on the
service. To change it, set a new value; to
learn the live value, read the service in the
Aiven Console.

Broker defaults in this block also apply to
topics. For example,
`kafka.log_retention_bytes` sets the broker
default for the topic setting
`retention.bytes`, which every topic without
its own value uses. That limit counts per
partition ([Kafka topic settings](https://kafk
a.apache.org/39/generated/topic_config.html)).

the-topic-name-is-the-key.wrapped_text:
The Topic Name Is the Key
An `aiven_kafka_topic` is known by three
fields: `project`, `service_name` and
`topic_name`. A change to any of them forces a
new topic ([topic fields](https://github.com/a
iven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/v4.66.0/doc
s/resources/kafka_topic.md#L84-L87)). Kafka
cannot rename a topic, so the old topic and
its messages are deleted.

The provider also refuses two changes at plan
time ([plan checks](https://github.com/aiven/t
erraform-provider-aiven/blob/v4.66.0/internal/
plugin/service/kafkatopic/topic.go#L161-L186))
:

- A smaller `partitions` value fails with
"number of partitions cannot be decreased".
- A new topic resource whose name already
exists in the service fails with "topic
conflict, already exists".

The `config` block holds only the topic
settings that you set. Removing the block does
not reset the topic: it keeps its last values 
([config](https://github.com/aiven/terraform-p
rovider-aiven/blob/v4.66.0/docs/resources/kafk
a_topic.md#L91)).

a-connector-is-a-map-of-strings.wrapped_text:
A Connector Is a Map of Strings
An `aiven_kafka_connector` runs one Kafka
Connect connector on a Connect service. Its
`config` is one flat map of strings, the same
keys that the Connect REST API takes. The
provider checks only one thing: `config.name`
must equal `connector_name` ([name check](http
s://github.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/
blob/v4.66.0/internal/sdkprovider/service/kafk
a/kafka_connector.go#L115-L129)). It accepts
any other key, including keys that Kafka
Connect ignores.

A refresh copies the live configuration into
the state, and an update sends the whole map.
The resource has no field for task health, so
a plan cannot show a connector whose tasks
have failed. The [Kafka map](../../kafka/kafka
.md#kafka-connect-service-aiven-kafka-connect)
explains where Connect runs on Aiven.
a-connector-is-a-map-of-strings.wrapped_original_text:

It accepts any other key, including keys that Kafka Connect ignores.

schema-subjects-only-grow.wrapped_text:
Schema Subjects Only Grow
An `aiven_kafka_schema` stands for one subject
in the Schema Registry, which Aiven runs with
Karapace ([Karapace](../../kafka/kafka.md#kara
pace-karapace)). A subject is a list of schema
versions. An edit to the schema in Terraform
registers a new version; it never rewrites an
old one. The plan checks the new schema
against the version in the state, and it fails
with "schema is not compatible with previous
version" when the check fails ([schema resourc
e](https://github.com/aiven/terraform-provider
-aiven/blob/v4.66.0/internal/sdkprovider/servi
ce/kafkaschema/kafka_schema.go#L444-L501)).

The compatibility rule comes from
`compatibility_level` on the subject, or from
the registry-wide
`aiven_kafka_schema_configuration`. Destroying
that resource sets the global level back to
BACKWARD ([schema configuration](https://githu
b.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/v4.6
6.0/internal/sdkprovider/service/kafkaschema/k
afka_schema_configuration.go#L129-L150)).

two-acl-models.wrapped_text:
Two ACL Models
An ACL is an access control list: a rule that
lets a service user do something. Aiven has
two kinds ([ACLs](https://aiven.io/docs/produc
ts/kafka/concepts/acl)):

- Aiven ACLs, with `aiven_kafka_acl`. Each
grants `read`, `write`, `readwrite` or `admin`
on topics. Users and topics can use wildcards.
- Kafka-native ACLs, with
`aiven_kafka_native_acl`. They follow Apache
Kafka's own model, with `ALLOW` and `DENY`
rules on more kinds of resources.

Both apply at the same time, and a `DENY` rule
wins over any grant. In Aiven ACLs, `*`
matches zero or more characters and `?`
matches exactly one. The Schema Registry has
its own ACLs, in
`aiven_kafka_schema_registry_acl`.

two-libraries-in-one-provider.wrapped_text:
Two Libraries in One Provider
The provider combines two Terraform libraries:
the older SDKv2 and the newer Plugin Framework
(PF). Aiven moves resources to PF one at a
time. After a move, a resource stores only the
values that you set, and it drops blocks that
your configuration does not have ([upgrade gui
de](https://github.com/aiven/terraform-provide
r-aiven/blob/v4.66.0/docs/guides/upgrade-guide
-v3-to-v4.md#L104-L191)). The first plan after
such an upgrade can therefore show changes
that remove blocks. Aiven says that applying
them is safe.

| Resource | Moved to PF in |
| --- | --- |
| `aiven_kafka_schema_registry_acl` | 4.57.0 |
| `aiven_kafka_topic` | 4.59.0 |
| `aiven_kafka_acl`, `aiven_kafka_native_acl`,
`aiven_kafka_user` | 4.61.0 |
| `aiven_service_integration`,
`aiven_service_integration_endpoint` | 4.66.0
|

The table comes from the [changelog](https://g
ithub.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/
v4.66.0/CHANGELOG.md). `aiven_kafka`,
`aiven_kafka_connect`,
`aiven_kafka_connector`, the schema resources
and `aiven_project` were still on SDKv2 in
4.66.0. Each release marks such changes with
**IMPORTANT** in the changelog.

aiven-changes-things-too.wrapped_text:
Aiven Changes Things Too
Aiven operates the services, so some changes
happen outside Terraform:

- Maintenance updates install the latest
connector plugin when no version is pinned
([connector versions](https://aiven.io/docs/pr
oducts/kafka/kafka-connect/howto/manage-connec
tor-versions)).
- Aiven issues new service-user certificates
about three months before they expire. The
certificates are valid for 820 days ([renew ce
rtificates](https://aiven.io/docs/products/kaf
ka/howto/renew-ssl-certs)).
- The power state of a service is outside
Terraform. You turn a service on or off in the
Aiven Console or the CLI ([state](https://gith
ub.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/v4.
66.0/docs/resources/kafka.md#L87)).
- After a power cycle, Aiven restores topics,
users, ACLs, schemas and Connect settings from
a configuration backup. It does not restore
the messages in classic topics ([configuration
backups](https://aiven.io/docs/products/kafka/
concepts/configuration-backup)).

None of these changes shows in a plan before
it happens.

Import ID |

`PROJECT/SERVICE_NAME/USERNAME` |
| `aiven_kafka_acl`, `aiven_kafka_native_acl`

| `aiven_kafka_connector` | connector | Target service, secrets in `config`, stable `connector_name` | `PROJECT/SERVICE_NAME/CONNECTOR_NAME` |

The import IDs come from the Import section of each [resource doc](https://github.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/tree/v4.66.0/docs/resources). Aiven generates the ID of an ACL, so you find it in the console or the API before an import.

aiven-where-to-look-first.wrapped_text:
Where to Look First
Read an Aiven configuration in this order:

1. `required_providers` and the lock file. The
version decides which resources use which
library, and which IMPORTANT changelog notes
apply.
2. The `provider "aiven"` block and the token
behind it. The token decides which projects
Terraform can reach and whether it can read
secrets.
3. The `aiven_kafka` and `aiven_kafka_connect`
blocks. Find where `project` and
`service_name` come from, because they are the
identity. Then read `plan`,
`termination_protection`, `lifecycle` and
`kafka_user_config`.
4. The `for_each` keys of topics, ACLs and
connectors. A changed key without a `moved`
block plans a destroy and a create.
5. The topics. Check `partitions`,
`replication` and the `config` keys. Note
topics that other tools also create, such as
dead-letter topics of connectors.
6. The ACLs. Check how far each wildcard
reaches, and which users exist outside
Terraform.
7. The schemas and the registry-wide
compatibility level.
8. The connectors. Check the target service,
secrets in `config`, `depends_on` on ACLs, and
plugin version pins.
9. The integrations and endpoints, and the
outputs that other code reads.

aiven-plan-signals.wrapped_text:
Plan Signals
| Line in the plan | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `-/+ aiven_kafka ... # forces replacement` |
The service and all its data will be deleted,
and every child object replaced. |
| `-/+ aiven_kafka_topic ... # forces
replacement` | The topic and its messages will
be deleted. |
| `number of partitions cannot be decreased` |
The plan stops; Kafka cannot remove
partitions. |
| `topic conflict, already exists` | A topic
with this name exists outside this resource:
import it, or add a `moved` block. |
| `schema is not compatible with previous
version` | The schema edit breaks the
compatibility rule. |
| `~` on a connector `config` without a code
change | Someone changed the connector outside
Terraform; the apply will revert it. |
| `~` on integrations right after a provider
upgrade | A resource moved to the Plugin
Framework; see the changelog's IMPORTANT
notes. |

service-replacement.wrapped_text:
Service Replacement
A new `service_name` or `project`, for example
from a typo in an input file, replaces the
Kafka service. Every topic, ACL and connector
inside it is replaced too.
`termination_protection` makes the delete fail
in Aiven, and `lifecycle { prevent_destroy =
true }` makes the plan fail before anything
runs. The old topic-level
`termination_protection` is checked only by
the provider, and only at apply ([issue 1596](
https://github.com/aiven/terraform-provider-ai
ven/issues/1596)). Use `prevent_destroy`
instead, as the topic docs advise ([topic docs
](https://github.com/aiven/terraform-provider-
aiven/blob/v4.66.0/docs/resources/kafka_topic.
md#L94)).

topic-identity.wrapped_text:
Topic Identity
A rename in the code deletes the topic with
its messages and creates an empty one. A
changed `for_each` key without a `moved` block
plans the same. When the new topic has the
same name, the plan fails with "topic
conflict, already exists". The same error
appears when a tool such as Kafka Connect
already created the topic, for example a
dead-letter topic. In that case, import the
topic.

partition-changes.wrapped_text:
Partition Changes
Raising `partitions` is an in-place change,
but it changes where keys go. The producer
picks the partition as `hash(key) %
partitions` ([Kafka partitioner](https://githu
b.com/apache/kafka/blob/4.1.0/clients/src/main
/java/org/apache/kafka/clients/producer/intern
als/BuiltInPartitioner.java#L329-L330)), and
Kafka does not move existing records ([Kafka o
perations](https://github.com/apache/kafka/blo
b/b87eb4f673075dc7bb410443689241fcb0302560/doc
s/operations/basic-kafka-operations.md#L59)).
This table uses Kafka's own hash function,
from About the Sources:

| Key | Partition with 3 partitions |
Partition with 6 partitions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `truck-17` | 2 | 2 |
| `truck-42` | 2 | 5 |
| `truck-88` | 1 | 4 |

After the change, new records for `truck-42`
go to partition 5, while its older records
stay in partition 2. A consumer that needs all
events of one key in order can then read a
newer event before an older one.

aiven-connector-pitfalls.wrapped_text:
Connector Pitfalls
These pitfalls do not show as errors. The
connector runs, but not as the code says.
aiven-connector-pitfalls.wrapped_original_text:
Connector Pitfalls
These pitfalls do not show as errors. The connector runs, but not as the code says.

secrets-in-connector-config.wrapped_text:
Secrets in Connector Config
The provider stopped marking connector
`config` as sensitive in 4.2.0 ([changelog](ht
tps://github.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aive
n/blob/v4.66.0/CHANGELOG.md#L1399)). A plan
prints each value that does not come from a
sensitive variable, and the state stores every
value in plain text. In Aiven, any user with
`service:data:write` can read connector
configurations, which "can contain secrets in
plain text" ([permissions](https://aiven.io/do
cs/platform/concepts/permissions)). Kafka
Connect secret providers keep the value out:
the config holds a reference to AWS Secrets
Manager instead ([secret providers](https://ai
ven.io/docs/products/kafka/kafka-connect/howto
/configure-secret-providers)).
secrets-in-connector-config.wrapped_original_text:

The provider stopped marking connector `config` as sensitive in 4.2.0 ([changelog](https://github.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/v4.66.0/CHANGELOG.md#L1399)). In Aiven, any user with `service:data:write` can read connector configurations, which "can contain secrets in plain text" ([permissions](https://aiven.io/docs/platform/concepts/permissions)). Kafka Connect secret providers keep the value out: the config holds a reference to AWS Secrets Manager instead ([secret providers](https://aiven.io/docs/products/kafka/kafka-connect/howto/configure-secret-providers)).

connector-drift.wrapped_text:
Connector Drift
An edit in the Aiven Console shows in the next
plan, and the apply reverts it. For example,
the console option for automatic restart is
the key `_aiven.restart.on.failure` in the
connector config ([provider example](https://g
ithub.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/
v4.66.0/examples/postgres/postgres_debezium_ka
fka/debezium_connector.tf#L24)); put it in the
code to keep it. A change of `connector_name`
or `service_name` creates a new connector. A
sink connector reads with the consumer group
`connect-<connector name>` ([Kafka source](htt
ps://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/4.1.0/connec
t/runtime/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/conne
ct/util/SinkUtils.java#L39-L41)). So a new
name starts a new group with no saved offsets,
and it reads the topic again from its
configured start point.
connector-drift.wrapped_original_text:

An edit in the Aiven Console shows in the next plan, and the apply reverts it. A change of `connector_name` or `service_name` creates a new connector. A sink connector reads with the consumer group `connect-<connector name>` ([Kafka source](https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/4.1.0/connect/runtime/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/connect/util/SinkUtils.java#L39-L41)). So a new name starts a new group with no saved offsets, and it reads the topic again from its configured start point.

keys-that-connect-ignores.wrapped_text:
Keys That Kafka Connect Ignores
The provider accepts any key, and Kafka's
config classes only log unused keys at info
level ([AbstractConfig](https://github.com/apa
che/kafka/blob/4.1.0/clients/src/main/java/org
/apache/kafka/common/config/AbstractConfig.jav
a#L386-L391)). So a misplaced setting does
nothing, and no error says so. Two examples:

- A consumer setting for one connector needs
the prefix `consumer.override.`, for example
`consumer.override.max.poll.records` ([Kafka
Connect user guide](https://github.com/apache/
kafka/blob/b87eb4f673075dc7bb410443689241fcb03
02560/docs/kafka-connect/user-guide.md#L57)).
- `offset.flush.interval.ms` is a worker
setting. It is not a connector setting
([worker settings](https://kafka.apache.org/39
/generated/connect_config.html)).

Aiven also says that `plugin_version` inside a
connector config has no effect ([connector ver
sions](https://aiven.io/docs/products/kafka/ka
fka-connect/howto/manage-connector-versions)).

unpinned-plugin-versions.wrapped_text:
Unpinned Plugin Versions
Without a pin, Aiven installs the latest
connector plugin version during maintenance,
and it can remove deprecated versions
([connector versions](https://aiven.io/docs/pr
oducts/kafka/kafka-connect/howto/manage-connec
tor-versions)). A connector can then change
behavior with no code change. The pin lives on
the service, not on the connector:
`plugin_versions` in
`kafka_connect_user_config` of a Connect
service, or `kafka_connect_plugin_versions` in
`kafka_user_config` when Connect runs on the
Kafka nodes ([Connect service doc](https://git
hub.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/v4
.66.0/docs/resources/kafka_connect.md#L125)).
A new pin restarts Kafka Connect.

connectors-before-integration.wrapped_text:
Connectors Before Their Integration
A dedicated Connect service reaches Kafka
through an `aiven_service_integration` of type
`kafka_connect`. The provider's docs give the
order: the Kafka service, the topics, the
Connect service, the integration, and then the
connectors ([setup order](https://github.com/a
iven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/v4.66.0/int
ernal/sdkprovider/service/kafka/kafka_connect.
go#L16-L26)). A connector that refers only to
the Connect service name has no dependency on
the integration. Add `depends_on` on the
integration, so Terraform keeps this order.

floating-provider-version.wrapped_text:
Floating Provider Version
A constraint such as `>= 4.46.0` with no
committed lock file installs each new release
on the next run. Release 4.66.0, for example,
moved integrations to the Plugin Framework, so
their first plan can show removed blocks. It
also fails the plan when one side of an
integration sets both an endpoint ID and a
service name ([4.66.0 notes](https://github.co
m/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/v4.66.0/
CHANGELOG.md#L15-L33)). Commit
`.terraform.lock.hcl`, and raise the version
on purpose.

schema-registry-edits.wrapped_text:
Schema Registry Edits
The plan checks a schema edit only against the
version in the state. With a `*_TRANSITIVE`
level, or with versions that producers
registered themselves, the plan can pass and
the apply can fail. Removing
`compatibility_level` from a subject keeps its
last value. Renaming the subject or changing
`schema_type` deletes the subject softly and
registers it again ([schema doc](https://githu
b.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/v4.6
6.0/docs/resources/kafka_schema.md#L6)).

acl-matching.wrapped_text:
ACL Matching
In an Aiven ACL, `*` matches zero or more
characters, dots included. So the topic
pattern `orders.*` also matches
`orders.dlq.retry`. Every field of an ACL
forces a new resource, so an edit deletes the
rule and then creates the new one, with a
short gap in between ([ACL fields](https://git
hub.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/v4
.66.0/docs/resources/kafka_acl.md#L40-L44)). A
new service also has a default ACL that gives
`avnadmin` the `admin` right on all topics.

the provider first checks that the service is
running ([service check](https://github.com/ai

rnal/schemautil/service.go#L1365-L1410)). A

the state and is planned again ([topic doc](ht
tps://github.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aive
n/blob/v4.66.0/docs/resources/kafka_topic.md#L
10)). Aiven deletes a service that stays off
for more than 180 days ([power off](https://ai
ven.io/docs/platform/concepts/service-power-cy
cle)).

The provider asks the Aiven API for secrets
when it reads some resources, such as service
users and integration endpoints. From 1 March
2027 the API redacts secrets unless the
token's role may read them ([4.66.0 notes](htt

edaction](https://aiven.io/docs/tools/api/secr
et-redaction)). A token without such a role
then makes these plans fail. The environment
variable `AIVEN_INCLUDE_SECRETS=false` reads
the resources without secrets.

dedicated-or-shared-connect.wrapped_text:
Dedicated or Shared Connect
Kafka Connect can run on the nodes of the
Kafka service or in a dedicated Connect
service ([enable Kafka Connect](https://aiven.
io/docs/products/kafka/kafka-connect/howto/ena
ble-connect)). On the Kafka nodes it costs
nothing extra, but it shares CPU and memory
with the brokers and needs a business or
premium plan. A dedicated service costs more
and scales on its own. The trade-off is cost
against the stability of the brokers. Moving a
connector between the two recreates it, so
choose before the first apply.

service-users-in-code-or-by-hand.wrapped_text:
Service Users in Code or by Hand
`aiven_kafka_user` puts each service user in
code, with drift detection. Its password and
access key then sit in the state in plain
text, and write-only arguments need Terraform
1.11 or later ([storing passwords](https://git
hub.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/v4
.66.0/docs/guides/storing-passwords.md)).
Users made by hand keep secrets out of the
state, but nothing checks them, and the ACLs
refer to names that Terraform cannot see.
Either way, certificate renewal is a manual
step ([renew certificates](https://aiven.io/do
cs/products/kafka/howto/renew-ssl-certs)).

Service Users in Code or by Hand
`aiven_kafka_user` puts each service user in code, with drift detection. Its password and access key then sit in the state in plain text, and write-only arguments need Terraform 1.11 or later ([storing passwords](https://github.com/aiven/terraform-provider-aiven/blob/v4.66.0/docs/guides/storing-passwords.md)). Users made by hand keep secrets out of the state, but nothing checks them, and the ACLs refer to names that Terraform cannot see. Either way, certificate renewal is a manual step ([renew certificates](https://aiven.io/docs/products/kafka/howto/renew-ssl-certs)).

Secret References over Secret Values
A connector config can hold a secret value, or
a reference that Kafka Connect resolves at run
time from AWS Secrets Manager or from
environment variables ([secret providers](http
s://aiven.io/docs/products/kafka/kafka-connect
/howto/configure-secret-providers)). The
reference keeps the secret out of the state,
the plan and the connector API. It costs one
more setup step on the Connect service.

One Project per Environment
Aiven recommends separate projects for
environments such as development and
production ([organizations and projects](https
://aiven.io/docs/platform/concepts/orgs-units-
projects)). It also recommends one application
user, with its own token, for each tool
([application users](https://aiven.io/docs/pla
tform/concepts/application-users)). Then a
token for development cannot touch production,
and each token can be rotated alone. One
shared token for all environments is simpler,
but it gives every pipeline the rights of all
of them.

About the Sources
The provider facts come from the `aiven/aiven`
repository at tag v4.66.0, the latest release on
2026-11-23. The Aiven facts come from aiven.io/docs
on the same day.

The partition table comes from this Python script.
It copies Kafka's `murmur2` function and its
default partitioner, and it checks itself against
three test values from Kafka's own tests ([UtilsTes
t](https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/4.1.0/clien
ts/src/test/java/org/apache/kafka/common/utils/Util
sTest.java#L106-L118)):

```python
def murmur2(data: bytes) -> int:
length = len(data)
m, r = 0x5BD1E995, 24
h = (0x9747B28C ^ length) & 0xFFFFFFFF
for i in range(length // 4):
i4 = i * 4
k = data[i4] | data[i4 + 1] << 8 | data[i4 + 2] <<
16 | data[i4 + 3] << 24
k = (k * m) & 0xFFFFFFFF
k ^= k >> r
k = (k * m) & 0xFFFFFFFF
h = (h * m) & 0xFFFFFFFF
h ^= k
rest = length % 4
if rest == 3:
h ^= data[(length & ~3) + 2] << 16
if rest >= 2:
h ^= data[(length & ~3) + 1] << 8
if rest >= 1:
h ^= data[length & ~3]
h = (h * m) & 0xFFFFFFFF
h ^= h >> 13
h = (h * m) & 0xFFFFFFFF
h ^= h >> 15
return h - (1 << 32) if h & 0x80000000 else h


def partition(key: str, partitions: int) -> int:
return (murmur2(key.encode()) & 0x7FFFFFFF) %
partitions


assert murmur2(b"21") == -973932308
assert murmur2(b"foobar") == -790332482
assert murmur2(b"a-little-bit-long-string") ==
-985981536
for key in ["truck-17", "truck-42", "truck-88"]:
print(key, partition(key, 3), partition(key, 6))
```
